vignette: The ceiling tiles split first, a sound like wet canvas tearing. Arthur is sixty-three now, but he is forty-eight in that moment, standing in the corridor of the St. Jude regional hospital. The explosion rips through the east wing. Glass rains across his scrubs. For three hours, he works without thinking, his hands moving on their own-applying pressure, counting doses, guiding people into dark rooms. When the dust settles, he counts the dead. He remembers the young resident who doesn't make it to the stairwell. He remembers the smell of copper and smoke. He goes home that night and stands in his shower until the water runs cold, trying to wash the grit from his hair, but it stays. The years that follow are measured in small surrenders. He remains in medicine, eventually shifting to an outpatient clinic where the fluorescent lights hum at a steady frequency and the air is filtered. He tells himself it is a step toward normalcy, but the shift costs him pieces of his old identity. At home, his wife, Elena, notices the quiet changes first. He no longer takes the highway to work. He checks the exits in every restaurant, sits with his back to the wall, maps the seating chart before the hostess even speaks. He stops volunteering at the hospital's safety drills. When Elena mentions a community barbecue, he says he has charting to finish, though his desk is clean. He sleeps in fragments. When he does drift off, he wakes at the exact moment his daughter used to leave for college, his heart hammering against his ribs, the ghost of an air-raid siren pulling him upright. He stares at the ceiling, convinced the floor is trembling again, and waits for the shaking to stop. In his clinic, Arthur moves with deliberate precision. He listens to patients with intense focus, but his own body never fully settles. A dropped chart sends his shoulders hiking toward his ears. The automatic doors whoosh, and his breath catches. He has learned to swallow the startle before it reaches his face, to let his voice drop half an octave so it sounds steady when it is not. He still prescribes, still draws blood, but he avoids procedures that require prolonged immobility. The sight of a gurney track triggers a sudden tightness behind his sternum, and he must pause, place a hand on the doorframe, and count backward from ten until the pressure eases. He tells himself he is adapting to age, but the truth is the ground still feels unsteady beneath him. At home, he loves Elena, but he cannot name the space that has opened between them. He watches her laugh across the dinner table and feels like a stranger in his own house. He avoids grocery stores during evening hours. He leaves early from family gatherings, citing a phantom fatigue that no amount of rest can touch. In this room, Arthur sits with his hands folded tightly over his knees. He speaks of the days following the blast in fragmented sentences, the way the world keeps turning while his stillness remains. He describes the weight of a stethoscope that now feels too heavy to lift, how he used to hang it around his neck like a promise. He notes how he watches traffic from his office window, counting cars that pass too quickly, timing the gaps between them. He does not look at the clock. He does not check the door. He simply breathes, the rhythm of it shallow but steady, as he waits for the next question to land like a stone in still water. The air in the room feels thick, charged with everything he has not yet said. His shoulders slowly lower, inch by inch, as if testing the weight of the moment.
